content: Compression garments are specialized clothing items, such as socks, pantyhose, and sleeves, designed to provide support. These garments are particularly beneficial for individuals who are required to stand for extended periods or those with compromised blood circulation. They are available in varying levels of compression, with higher levels necessitating a prescription from a medical professional. When worn on the legs, compression garments can aid in the prevention of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and help reduce swelling, especially during travel. Additionally, compression tights are utilized by some athletes to enhance performance and recovery. The Australian Physiotherapy Association (APA) has officially endorsed Skins products. According to David Malone, the APA's Chief Executive Officer, this endorsement signifies that physiotherapists can now recommend Skins products, as they meet the rigorous standards required for APA endorsement. Research has demonstrated that wearing compression garments can result in higher mean skin temperatures, lower creatine kinase (CK) levels 24 hours post-exercise, and reduced muscle soreness ratings 24 hours post-exercise. These findings suggest potential benefits in recovery and performance. Material testing of compression garments has shown that they enhance joint flexion and extension, which may contribute to a reduction in hamstring injuries. Furthermore, these garments have been found to decrease impact forces by 27% compared to wearing standard American football pants alone. Studies, such as those published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine and the Journal of Sports Sciences, have evaluated the effects of compression garments on athletic performance and recovery. For instance, research by Duffield and Portus (2007) compared three types of full-body compression garments on throwing and repeat-sprint performance in cricket players. Another study by Doan et al. (2003) assessed the efficacy of lower-body compression garments, highlighting their potential benefits in sports and exercise contexts.
